#4432. Grad student finds New Mexico’s first Canada lynx in 25 years

Published Nov 13, 2026 11:00 AM EST

In June, New Mexico State University graduate student William Grooms was using motion-sensing cameras to investigate wildlife in Carson National Forest in northern New Mexico. And when he looked through his first images, he spotted something flabbergasting.

His cameras had captured a series of photographs of a Canada lynx (Lynx canadensis)—a wild cat that hasn’t been documented in the state for around 25 years. But Grooms had to make sure it wasn’t actually a bobcat (Lynx rufus), which is a similar-looking species.

“It caught my eye because the cat in the image had the characteristic ear tufts and facial ruff [of bobcats], but it was lacking the black spots that are typical of bobcats,” Grooms, who is studying in the department of Fish, Wildlife and Conservation Ecology, tells Popular Science. “We also have a good image of the tail, which on lynx has a solid black tip compared to a bobcat whose tail has white on the underside, so my confidence grew.”

He and his team also showed the image to other researchers for confirmation. Ultimately, there’s no doubt about the fact that the big cat slinking through the dark was indeed a Canada lynx. The species lives in dense boreal and subalpine forests and woodlands throughout much of Canada and Alaska. They have long legs, grayish or yellowish-brown coats, and wide fur-lined paws.

Their main prey are snowshoe hares (Lepus americanus), which they follow into the forest understory—the ground-level area of downed trees and dense vegetation beneath which the hares hide and live. The problem is that these kinds of habitats are fire hazards. Recent forest fire mitigation efforts include decreasing dangerous fuel loads via thinning, prescribed burning, or timber harvesting.

“While these tactics reduce the risk of severe fires, they also remove important habitat features,” Grooms explains. “Our objective is to provide managers with practical, science-based advice regarding what effects fuel reduction treatments and timber harvesting have on wildlife in the Southern Rocky Mountains so that they can make well-informed decisions as they go about their task of managing our nation’s forests.”

Simply knowing that at least one Canada lynx was in the area provides more data for this mission.

#4431. Tesla Cybercab’s autonomy agreement is insane: $299/mo or it doesn’t move

Tesla has posted the agreement that comes with its $29,990 Cybercab, and it’s even worse than the order page suggested. The two-seater can’t move without a $299 monthly “Autonomy Subscription” that Tesla can reprice with a month’s notice, suspend for a week, or cut off entirely.

And Tesla wants consumers to sign it while still refusing to give unsupervised self-driving to the Model Y owners it has been selling “Full Self-Driving” to for nearly a decade.

The “Cybercab Autonomy Subscription Agreement” (version 20261112) went up on Tesla’s configurator late Friday, hours after the company started inviting select customers to order the Cybercab for personal use at $29,990 plus a mandatory $299 per month.

The key line is short: “Your Cybercab will not operate without an active Autonomy Subscription.” There’s no steering wheel and no pedals, so that isn’t a figure of speech. Stop paying and you have a $30,000 object in your garage.

That personal-use clause kills the whole pitch. For years, Musk told people they’d buy a Tesla, add it to the fleet, and make money while they sleep. The first Tesla sold to consumers for unsupervised operation is contractually barred from doing exactly that.

Then there’s the geofence. Tesla’s Robotaxi service areas are already smaller in practice than advertised: when we tested them, real coverage was between 59% and 78% of the advertised maps, and parts of the Houston map have been called “fake” by the person tracking it. Now Tesla reserves the right to shrink that area after you’ve paid for the car.

Mark Valorian, who went through the terms on X, summed it up as “an endless variable-rate lease with a ridiculous down payment.” That’s about right.

Over five years, the car plus 59 paid months of subscription comes to $47,631 before insurance, registration, charging, and taxes, all of which are on the owner.

This is the part that should make every Tesla owner angry.

Tesla has spent the last year telling everyone that its Model Y is just as much a robotaxi as the Cybercab. Ahead of the Robotaxi launch in Austin, Musk said the cars were “the Model Ys we make currently, there’s no change to it.” On Tesla’s Q3 2026 earnings call last month, AI chief Ashok Elluswamy said Cybercabs and Model Y robotaxis already run the same software, and that customer cars might join the network around Q2 2027. The Cybercab launches on the same AI4 computer found in the current Model Y.

So the hardware is the same, the software is the same, and unsupervised Model Ys are already operating in the exact geofences where Cybercab owners will be allowed to ride.

Yet the people who paid for it get nothing. Tesla started selling “Full Self-Driving Capability” in 2016 on the promise that every car it built had the hardware for it. Owners paid up to $15,000 for the package. In February, Tesla stopped selling it outright and moved to a $99 per month subscription, which still requires you to supervise the car at all times.

Tesla’s answer to all those owners is a new car. One with two seats, no controls, a geofence it can move whenever it wants, and a subscription that costs three times as much as FSD.

I’ll say it plainly: this car is for suckers who want to give their money to Elon Musk.

You don’t own a Cybercab in any meaningful sense. You pay $30,000 for the right to keep paying Tesla $299 a month, at a price Tesla can raise, in an area Tesla can shrink, under rules Tesla enforces, with a camera pointed at you the whole time.

There are three possible reasons Tesla isn't allowing model Y owners to use FSD in the allowed zones:

1: the robotaxis are in fact different from the model Ys being sold

2: Tesla doesn't have enough "remote operators" to cover all of those supposedly self-driving cars if users join the network

3: Tesla isn't willing to accept liability when FSD kills someone.

And the Model Y part is what gives the game away. If Tesla truly believed its unsupervised system was ready for customers, the obvious move would be to turn it on for the Model Y owners in Austin who already paid for it. It’s the same computer and the same software in the same geofence. But that would mean honoring a promise made in 2016, on cars already sold, with no new revenue attached.

A new vehicle wipes that slate clean. No legacy FSD buyers, no HW3 baggage, just a fresh customer locked into a $299 monthly fee from day one. What Tesla built is a subscription with a $30,000 entry fee attached to it.

So what happens the first time Tesla emails Cybercab owners a month’s notice that the price is going to $399?

#4430. Ghosts don’t scare German shepherds

Published Nov 13, 2026 12:00 PM EST

The German shepherd was originally bred to do exactly what their name implies, but a lot has changed since Max von Stephanitz introduced the breed in 1899. Today, the German shepherd is one of the world’s most recognizable and popular dogs, largely due to their intelligence, trainability, and companionship. You’re just as likely to spot one of them at an airport sniffing for contraband as you are at a kennel club competition.

But a good “work” German shepherd and a good show dog require two very different sets of traits. According to researchers at Sweden’s Uppsala University, these specific qualities are so pronounced that they’re even visible at the genetic level. What’s more, many of these genes can also be seen in humans.

“It’s interesting that we can now see that this selective breeding has indeed led to differences between working dogs and show dogs among German shepherds—differences that can be seen at both the behavioral and genetic levels,” Uppsala University genomics researcher Kerstin Lindblad-Toh explained in a recent profile.

Lindblad-Toh and her colleagues laid out their findings in a study recently published in the journal Animal Genetics. To assess the iconic breed, the team reviewed a massive dataset of 23,000 German shepherds who previously participated in a standardized behavioral test known as the Dog Mentality Assessment (DMA). During the DMA, canines are exposed to a range of situations, such as meeting strangers, play time, and even encountering imposing, ghostly figures. The team discovered that while German shepherds often scored higher for traits like neuroticism and shyness, the breed’s working dogs generally exhibited more curiosity, less fear, and a willingness to socialize with people.

“Breeders of working dogs have selected and bred the ones that really enjoy working; it’s a bit like a game for them,” said Lindblad-Toh.

From there, the researchers gathered blood samples and mapped the genomes of 373 German shepherds who previously took the DMA. Some of these behavioral divergences were so stark that the study’s authors could pinpoint them in the dogs’ genetics.

“We could then see that there were areas in the genome where differences could be seen in the dogs depending on how curious or playful they were, for example,” Lindblad-Toh said. “That meant that we were able to identify some of the genes in working dogs that are linked to curiosity and playfulness.”

In some instances, the same genes influencing German shepherd personalities are also tied to the same behaviors in humans. This means it may be possible to further explore human psychology with the aid of our best animal friends. Although Lindblad-Toh cautioned that their study is “just a first step” along this path, they hope to learn more about specific breed genetic traits and their overlap with owners.

“We now have an example of how we might also acquire more knowledge about different behaviors in people with [the] help of dogs in the longterm,” she said.

#4429. Huawei set to challenge Tesla Powerwall with new, 20 kW home battery

This high-tech Huawei home battery pack hopes to hold back Tesla’s latest Powerwall with silicon carbide technology, AI-powered energy management baked in, and enough modular storage to keep even large homes bright and warm when the rest of the block goes dark.

Huawei believes its new Luterra S2 is more than just a home backup battery. The Chinese tech firm is calling it an “all-in-one residential energy system” that combines a hybrid inverter, modular battery storage, and AI-powered energy management in a single, simple, and stackable package that’s available in single-phase versions that put out between 3 and 10 kW and three-phase versions that can push up to 20 kW.

The Luterra S2 is the first system of its kind to use Huawei’s proprietary full-silicon carbide (SiC) architecture, which promises improved efficiency, power density, and ease of use. It’s so easy, in fact, that Huawei claims it can be installed and commissioned in just minutes.

“We are thrilled to introduce Huawei Luterra S2, our next-generation all-in-one residential energy system,” said Steve Zhang, President of Huawei Distributed PV & BESS Business. “By combining full-SiC architecture, AI-driven energy management, and industry-leading safety, Luterra S2 is designed to be smaller, lighter, quieter, safer, smarter and more powerful than ever before.”

Huawei’s basic Luterra S2 configuration starts with “just” 5 kWh of battery energy storage and 3 kW of output. That’s enough to keep essential household appliances, lighting, and electronics running during a power outage, but you’ll want to keep going if you’re preparing for more than a day or two without power.

Keeping all that power cool and quiet is a Huawei-developed passive cooling system that does without external fans, keeping operating noise levels below a claimed 29 dB (about the same as my Mac mini). It operates at ambient temperatures from –25° C to about 60° C, and features a sturdy IP66-rated enclosure (safe to hit with a high-pressure hose) with corrosion protection up to C5-M to keep it from rusting away.

#4428. Mercedes-Benz’s New Driving-Assist Tech Puts Tesla on Notice

The German brand's MB.Drive Assist Pro is Mercedes’s answer to Full Self-Driving (Supervised).

If Tesla operates under the Silicon Valley mantra of "move fast and break things," then Mercedes, like most automotive players outside China, runs on "move steadily and avoid unnecessary liability." To wit, Mercedes took nearly half a dozen years to roll out a competing system to Tesla’s point-to-point automated driving system better known as Full Self-Driving (Supervised).

Dubbed MB.Drive Assist Pro, the automated driving technology allows so-equipped Mercedes models to accelerate, brake, steer, and respond to dynamic environmental features such as traffic lights, road signs, and nearby vehicles and pedestrians. With the aid of the automaker's aptly named Hands-Free Highway Assist, Mercedes models equipped with MB.Drive Assist Pro can handle the majority—if not all—of the tasks of driving with minimal input from the person behind the steering wheel.

See all results for used cars for sale near 06032

Mercedes is blunt about the capabilities of both systems and does not attempt to obfuscate the active role the driver plays when using these subscription-based services. Though it didn’t dive into specifics, the company stated it plans to give eligible customers access to the features for an undetermined trial period.

The automaker plans to initially launch these driver-assist tools in December 2026 to a limited number of California customers with select Mercedes models running the brand's MB.OS software via an over-the-air (OTA) update. Nationwide rollout follows in 2027 through an OTA update for current owners of compatible Mercedes models, new versions of which will be able to leave the lot with one or both features active.

Mercedes vehicles capable of supporting both MB.Drive Assist Pro and Hands-Free Highway Assist for 2027 include CLA-class (gas and electric), GLC-class EV, GLE-class, GLS-class, S-class, and 2026 CLA-class EV models equipped with the brand’s MB.Drive Assist suite of driver-assist features. Meanwhile, MB.Drive Assist-equipped 2027 GLB-class, C-class, gas-powered GLC-class, EQS-class Sedan, and AMG GT 4-Door models will support Hands-Free Highway Assist but not MB.Drive Assist Pro.

Earlier this year, Mercedes invited us to San Francisco to experience MB.Drive Assist Pro automated driving system from the passenger seat. Less than 12 months later, we returned to the Bay Area to experience the tech from the driver's seat of an all-wheel-drive GLC400 EV.

See all results for used cars for sale near 06032

Once activated, MB.Drive Assist Pro puttered the battery-powered Benz around north San Francisco with smooth but cautious inputs. If early iterations of Full Self-Driving (Supervised) reacted with the timidity and hesitancy of a new driver, MB.Drive Assist Pro approached the dense urban environment of San Fran like an experienced driver playing the part of a diffident tourist visiting the area for the first time.

For instance, after successfully stopping for a red light at an intersection with a busy crosswalk, MB.Drive Assist Pro struggled to take off after the light turned green. Instead, it ever so slowly crept forward before applying the brakes again the moment its various cameras and sensors detected movement from a pedestrian standing at either end of the crosswalk ahead, seemingly interpreting such motions as an intent by the individual to enter the crosswalk. Getting across the intersection ultimately required us to temporarily override the system with a quick boot of the right pedal.

A second such incident occurred a few minutes later when the battery-powered Benz encountered a truck standing in our lane. MB.Drive Assist Pro navigated around this obstacle by swiftly entering and exiting the opposing lane of this narrow two-way road. Once clear of the truck, the dual-motor Mercedes spotted a stop sign ahead. The electric SUV slowed to a halt before fully reentering its lane. Again, we overrode MB.Drive Assist Pro with a nudge of the accelerator, which brought every bit of the Benz out of the way of oncoming traffic.

Between its occasional need for overrides and its inability to operate completely hands-free, MB.Drive Assist Pro certainly has room to improve. Even so, the system’s actions never left us feeling in danger or uncomfortable. Likewise, we quickly adapted to keeping a hand on the wheel while MB.Drive Assist Pro took charge of steering duties. Ideal? No. Acceptable? Yes.

Mercedes will let drivers go hands-free on the highway, though. We got a feel for the brand’s Hands-Free Driving Assist system from behind the wheel of a plug-in hybrid S580e, which we took across the San Francisco-Oakland Bay Bridge toward the East Bay and back.

Operating Hands-Free Driving Assist is by way of the brand’s usual cruise control layout. An instrument cluster graphic of a steering wheel lets drivers know whether or not hands-free driving is available.

As with other competing systems, Hands-Free Highway Assist can perform automatic lane changes. The Mercedes setup pulls these off with little drama, and will do so with or without the presence of the driver’s hands. Put a destination into the in-dash navigation system, and the lane-change function will guide you to your exit.

Stay vigilant around toll areas, though. We almost ran one after the plug-in Benz failed to clock the red stoplight overhead. Likewise, be ready to take over driving duty even on mildly curving stretches of highway. It’s arguably the most irritating characteristic of Hands-Free Driving Assist.

Neither Hands-Free Driving Assist nor MB.Drive Assist Pro are static services. Real-world driving data from these systems will allow Mercedes to regularly improve the performance of these driving-assist features. These updated parameters can then be sent directly to vehicles OTA. How quickly such software updates deploy will ultimately depend on how comfortable Mercedes is with breaking things.

#4427. How to Plan Your Holiday Meals in a Year of Unprecedented Recalls

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Following a series of high-profile food recalls and outbreaks this year, many Americans may be concerned about keeping their families safe from foodborne illness during the holidays.

In fact, according to a recent national survey by Orlando Health, around 60% of U.S. adults say they’re more concerned about foodborne illness this year than in previous years.

Although several major foodborne illness outbreaks have ended and their associated recalls are no longer active, food safety remains an important concern. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) estimates that 48 million people in the United States experience foodborne illness each year.

However, there are simple steps you can take to reduce the risk of foodborne illness when preparing holiday meals and storing leftovers.

While there were several food recalls in the United States over the summer, two of the largest involved Salmonella linked to jalapeños and Cyclospora linked to lettuce.

These outbreaks prompted widespread recalls and raised concerns about the safety of certain foods, particularly fresh produce.

Although health officials have since declared the major outbreaks over, some consumers may still be hesitant to purchase foods associated with previous recalls.

Even with this declaration, you may still feel nervous about purchasing certain foods, but experts say you don’t need to worry.

“Here in the United States, we have the safest food supply in the world. The recent recalls show that our food safety system is working,” said William Schaffner, MD, Professor, Division of Infectious Diseases at Vanderbilt University.

Michelle Routhenstein, preventive cardiology dietitian at Entirely Nourished, told Healthline that past recalls do not mean entire food categories need to be avoided. The important thing is whether the specific product you have matches a current recall, based on details such as brand, lot number, package size, and expiration date.

“You should enjoy familiar foods, including properly cooked poultry, washed fruits and vegetables, and pasteurized dairy products,” she said. “The key is checking relevant recalls and practicing safe food handling.”

“Before shopping or cooking, review FDA and USDA (U.S. Department of Agriculture) recall information and compare any relevant notices with the labels on your ingredients,” said Routhenstein.

Check the pantry and freezer, too: something purchased months ago may still be affected.

“Stay alert to any news reports about food recalls and use good food preparation practices. Those simple actions should keep your holidays happy and safe,” said Schaffner.

Consumers can sign up for food recall alerts through the FDA or visit FoodSafety.gov for recall information from both the FDA and USDA.

Schaffner emphasized the importance of following safe food-handling practices when preparing everyday meals and holiday gatherings.

“Remember the longstanding advice: keep food hot or cold. Avoid long times at room temperature,” he said.

Routhenstein advised focusing on four basics: clean, separate, cook, and chill.

Schaffner noted the importance of refrigerating leftovers promptly rather than leaving them at room temperature for extended periods. He recommends clearing the table and refrigerating leftovers soon after the meal ends.

Routhenstein reiterated that you should refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours rather than leaving them out to cool.

Divide turkey into smaller portions and transfer sides and gravy into shallow containers to help them cool quickly, she advised.

Leftovers can typically be stored in the refrigerator for 3–4 days. If you don’t plan to eat them within that time, consider freezing them.

The important thing is to keep an eye out for any new recalls, practice food safety, and enjoy your holiday meals!

#4426. Adventurous baby black bear wins 2026 Courageous Cub Award

Published Nov 13, 2026 1:09 PM EST

One little bear cub in Southeastern Alaska’s Tongass National Forest is a true model of bravery. The park’s rangers have awarded the unnamed black bear (Ursus americanus) cub with the 2026 Courageous Cub award for persevering when he got himself in a little pickle this summer. The cub belongs to a forgetful mother bear named Dory, who had two cubs this season.

“This little cub of Dory’s went on a big adventure. He got lost, ran down the trail a half mile and approached visitors as if to ask, ‘Are you my mommy?’ Then got scared and ran off in the wrong direction,” the Tongass rangers write. “Hours later he came running back up the trail sniffing out where mama was.”

Black bears like this family have a very keen sense of smell. It is debated just how far away they can smell, but it is at least two miles and could be up to 20. Fortunately, the cub was able to use some of that sniffing power to find both Dory and his other sibling.

The rangers at Tongass National Forest are currently awarding the Anan Bear Awards to the 39 bears spotted at the Anan Wildlife Observatory in Alaska over the summer.

Tongass is the largest national forest in the United States. It covers most of southeastern Alaska, including the state’s capital city of Juneau, and includes Mendenhall Glacier (a popular destination for Alaskan cruises), numerous hiking trails, eagles soaring above, and plenty of bears on the hunt for food. One of the hotspots is Anan Creek, home to one of the largest runs of pink salmon in Southeast Alaska. This makes the creek a very popular dinner spot among black and brown bears.

According to Friends of Anan, at least 39 bears feast on the salmon at Anan Creek. The population includes 31 black bears and eight brown bears (Ursus arctos). Similar to their chunky counterparts farther to the north in Katmai National Park, the bears return each summer to feast on salmon and teach their cubs how to fish in order to survive. And also like the fat bears of Katmai, every bear here has their own habits and quirks.

The U.S. Forest Service tracks and documents every bear spotted at Anan, while explore.org’s cameras broadcast live streams of their behavior.

#4425. Check your ego at the door: Stellantis’ new electric dolly turns ANY car into a tow rig

We all know the type: grizzled stubble, wraparound PitVipers, a MAGA hat quietly retired after last week’s deep-blue shellacking, and a pristine, polished pickup parked in the driveway that they “need for towing.” With Stellantis’ new patent for an AI-powered electric tow dolly that turns just about ANY vehicle into a capable tow rig, however, those might need a new to find a new excuse to keep that gas-guzzler.

Originally filed in 2023, Stellantis received US Patent No. 12,779,916 for its electric tow dolly on 03NOV2026. The patent covers a machine that’s designed to shoulder the trailer’s hitch load with its own ball hitch or fifth-wheel plate, using an on-board electric motor and battery to get the trailer going while its regenerative braking system and AI-backed steering and traction control system keeps everything pointed in the right direction.

In other words, the dolly takes on many of the jobs that traditionally require a big tow vehicle: providing the pulling power, managing the trailer’s weight and controlling its braking and traction. The vehicle up front doesn’t necessarily need a massive motor, heavy-duty suspension or oversized brakes. With a system like this, you could argue that the “tow vehicle” isn’t really a tow vehicle at all. It’s more of a “lead vehicle,” since the dolly is the one doing the towing … and it can follow just about anything – including the diminutive (and supremely affordable) Fiat 500e, which is also made by Stellantis.

To be clear, this isn’t just Uncle Jojo making fun of the commuter conveys – Stellantis’ patent describes the dolly as being equipped with an autonomous control system using cameras, sensors, a controller, and an advanced, four wheel steer-by-wire system. It also specifically discusses how the dolly’s independently powered acceleration, braking and steering, and sway controls essentially remove the need to own a truck in the first place.

The dolly system’s truck bed sides and small size allow users to experience the functionality and utility of a truck only when they need it, allowing them to own a smaller, cheaper, and more fuel efficient vehicle that suits daily use needs.

There are some pretty obvious practical questions still to answer, of course, including how much battery capacity the dolly would need, how much weight it could handle and how it would perform on long grades or in emergency braking situations. And, to be clear, a patent isn’t a product announcement or proof that Stellantis plans to put one of these things on sale – heck, if I were Stellantis’ CEO, I’d patent this thing just to prevent anyone else from building one so I could keep selling ancient, low-tech, high-margin Ram Trucks – but it’s a neat idea.

Okay, I like this idea and appreciate the problem it is trying to solve, but it has the same challenge as any electric-tow situation, which is the charging logistics. Even if you find a pull-through charger (very rare), if you are using an EV, you still need to charge two "vehicles," so you have to charge your car, then pull up and charge the dolly afterwards. Even if you are using a gas car, charging the dolly will be logistically challenging. Of course, that's a problem with an easy solution (more pull-through chargers), but also one that doesn't seem to be on any charging network's radar.

I think it’s neat, anyway. What do you guys think? Are you ready to trade in your big-battery Chevy Silverado EV or Volvo VNR 800 on a new Topolino, or are you going to keep driving inefficient 99% of the time? Let us know, in the comments.

#4424. The New Smaller Land Rover Defender Will Arrive First as an EV

Likely called the Defender Sport, this electric downsized Defender will ride on the same platform as the Range Rover GT.

At Jaguar Land Rover, the word Sport essentially means “fun size.” Full-size Range Rover? That’s just a Range Rover. The wee version that’s a bit nippier through the bends? That’ll be the Range Rover Sport. Now, with the Defender getting its own scaled-down Sport version, it’s going to be electric.

Now, there’s still a chance that this smaller Defender model could be named something other than Sport, as JLR head PB Balaji has been a little cagey about explicitly calling the upcoming car Defender Sport. Speaking on JLR’s second earnings call, he confirmed that the factory that currently builds the Discovery Sport and Evoque will be manufacturing the new Defender and the Range Rover GT starting next year.

See all results for Land Rover Defender Sport for sale near 29405

The two cars will share JLR’s new Electrified Modular Architecture platform, which is designed to support 800-volt electric vehicles and also hybrids. However, Balaji indicated that only the battery-electric small Defender would be ready to go by the end of next year.

Pretty much everything in JLR’s range (leaving out the rebooting Jaguar brand) has pretty impressive off-road chops, but a Defender Sport has to be particularly special. It’s one thing to offer a smaller, more agile Range Rover Sport that has most of the luxury of the full-size vehicle with better agility. This new model will be the first in a planned series of vehicles that will establish Defender not just as a single product but as a brand.

JLR probably can’t get away with how Ford positions the Bronco and the Bronco Sport as a Jeep Wrangler competitor and an Escape crossover, respectively, with more personality. The Defender Sport might be smaller than its big brother, but it’s going to need to offer up most of the same off-road chops.

As distinct from the electric version of the Mercedes-Benz G-class, which tucked its batteries onboard in such a way as to offer up all of the same ability as the combustion-powered versions, the Defender Sport’s EMA setup utilizes underfloor batteries. JLR’s Mark Cameron, who heads up the Discovery and Defender brands, admitted that there may be a slight reduction in wheel travel and articulation versus a full-size Defender.

Then again, few owners are using the full capabilities of their Defenders on the regular, even if they really are landed English gentry roving around their untamed huge tracts of land. A lot of the Defender’s ability isn’t just mechanical doggedness, like an old Series Land Rover, but clever terrain-management software. All of that suite of abilities should port over.

See all results for Land Rover Defender Sport for sale near 29405

A smaller Defender, even one that’s perhaps not quite ready to take on the Dakar Rally, does sound like plenty of fun, especially on narrower trails. Given how successful the current Defender model has been for JLR as a whole, it probably can’t get here fast enough.

#4423. Divers release first footage of SS ‘United States’ after intentional sinking

Published Nov 13, 2026 2:00 PM EST

It took a few hours longer than expected, but the SS United States now rests at the bottom of the Gulf of Mexico. The nearly 1,000-foot-long ocean liner sank off the coast of Pensacola, Florida, to a depth of about 190 feet on November 11, where it is now officially the world’s largest artificial reef. In the years ahead, biologists and conservationists will monitor the vessel’s remains as numerous marine species slowly convert the ship into their own home.

Ahead of the next phase in the United States’ recycled life, divers from the RV Explorer swam to document the vessel’s location and post-scuttling condition. On November 13, the team released a brief video of their successful excursion. Interestingly, the footage shows the ship is resting upright on the ocean floor despite initially sinking on its side.

“It was just epic,” diver Rustin Cassway told a local Philadelphia news outlet. “It was very cleaned up. I mean, you could see people really took their time to clean it really nicely.”

The project marks the first time ecologists will be able to monitor a shipwreck’s transformation in real-time. Researchers now plan to conduct annual visits to the SS United States to chart not only the artificial reef’s progress, but how the ship’s materials may affect the surrounding ocean conditions.

In its heyday, the SS United States was the world’s fastest ocean liner. Larger than the RMS Titanic, she was the most powerful, advanced, and modern passenger liner when she first took to the ocean in 1952. In addition to the 1,700 passengers, 7,935 quarts of ice cream and 500 pounds of caviar were also on board. During that maiden voyage (July 3-7, 1952), she broke the transatlantic speed record held by the RMS Queen Mary by over 10 hours. The United States made the crossing from the United Kingdom to New York in three days, 10 hours, and 40 minutes at an average speed of 40.96 mph.

She was designed by naval architect William Francis Gibbs (August 24, 1886 – September 6, 1967), and was built to be converted into a troopship if the United States Navy needed during a time of war. But she never was called into military service. Instead, the United States transported immigrants and celebrities, including future President and First Lady John and Jacqueline Kennedy, actors Grace Kelly, Gary Cooper, and Marilyn Monroe, artist Salvador Dali, and musicians Duke Ellington and Irving Berlin. Walt Disney even filmed parts of the 1962 comedy Bon Voyage aboard the ship.

An engineering marvel, some of the key design features were in the rudder, radar mast, and propellers.

The rudder was designed for good maneuverability at high speeds. The Titanic’s relatively small rudder was one factor behind the ship’s collision with an iceberg and tragic sinking in 1912.

The SS United States had the latest radar equipment, which allowed the crew to see the locations of  other ships and objects in the ocean despite the weather. It was among the first ocean liners to use radar, which was located at one of the highest points on the ship, so in addition to her radar “eyes,” a lookout could be stationed there to warn the captain of any danger in the ship’s path.

Considered a top-secret design, the ship had four propellers—two with four blades and two with five. According to the SS United States Conservancy, this configuration was tested and selected for its superior hydrodynamic performance. The propeller design was overseen by a pioneering Gibbs & Cox engineer named Elaine Kaplan.

Ocean liners became a less attractive option once air travel became quicker and less expensive. The SS United States ceased operations in 1969, and stayed in drydock in several cities before becoming the world’s largest artificial reef.

#4422. $20K Nissan NX7 PHEV goes on sale with nearly 200 miles of electric range

Dongfeng Nissan officially opened the early order book on its new NX7 hybrid yesterday, promising up to 320 km (~198 miles) of all-electric range from a 40 kWh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery and a $20,000 price tag.

When the first generation Nissan LEAF bowed with 70-ish miles of range from its 24 kWh li-ion battery pack, it struggled to meet widespread adoption, especially in an SUV-obsessed US market that demands forethought-free trips to Home Depot and bladder-busting range. The company’s latest 2027 Rogue Hybrid is a step in the right direction, using a gas engine to generate electricity for a pair of electric drive motors that deliver a driving experience that’s remarkably similar to a “pure” electric car – but without a plug, it’s still entirely dependent on fossil fuels. The new Dongfeng Nissan NX7, though? That’s a different story.

The plug-in hybrid Dongfeng Nissan NX7 might be called a “long range hybrid” in the same sense that Volvo’s Euro-market XC70 is, in that it’s an EV for the 360-odd days a year that you’re driving less than 200 miles, and an ICE vehicle for the handful of days you drive more. And if you’re one of those people who thinks stopping on road trips is a character flaw, a fully charged and topped off NX7 will take you an astonishing 1,666 km (~1,035 miles) from where you started.

The new NX7 could be an ideal lilypad vehicle for North American drivers who are either too afraid of being caught without a charger or too invested in the outcome of one or more dumb oil wars to confidently make the switch to EV – and, even at twice the 129,900 yuan ($~19,400) asking price, I think it would be a hit.

For that money, NX7 buyers get an absolutely loaded Model Y-sized crossover (they’re within 1/4″ of each other in length), with a 17.3″ central touchscreen, a fully digital instrument cluster, and (on higher-spec models) a positively massive 55″ augmented-reality head-up display powered by Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 8295P automotive processor and running on Nissan OS 3.0 with an AI-powered voice assistant developed with iFlytek that, Nissan claims, can recognize natural-language commands, remember user preferences, and even recognize occupants, adjusting vehicle settings accordingly.

On top-shelf models, the NX7 cabins get “AI Zero-Pressure Cloud Blanket” seats that use sensors and air-cushion arrays to dynamically adjust for maximum comfort, and include heating, ventilation, and a 12-point SPA-level massage function. The front seats can be fully reclined to create a bed-like configuration that will be familiar to Cube owners. The NX7 even offers an on-board refrigerator and motion-sickness prevention system that Nissan claims can reduce motion sickness by as much as 83% (which, like, I wouldn’t want to be the one to test that – but seems cool).

Power comes from a 1.5-liter naturally aspirated internal combustion engine making 98 hp that’s paired to a 228 hp electric drive motor and the previously mentioned 40.9 kWh LFP battery. It’s not immediately clear if the NX7 uses a conventional parallel hybrid system like a Prius or a series-hybrid-plus-plug setup, but Dongfeng’s hybrid technology patents describe a pretty versatile arrangement with four possible operating modes: series hybrid, parallel hybrid, direct engine drive and electricity generation – which means the vehicle can theoretically use the ICE motor as a generator, drive the wheels mechanically, or work alongside the electric motor, depending on what the operating conditions call for. Whether any or all four modes make it to production on the NX7 remains to be seen, but it’s an intriguing bit of engineering for a vehicle promising nearly 200 miles of electric driving range.

Why is this article written like it will be available in the US market? It’s made in China and has Chinese software, we’ll never see it

The final production version will be shown to the public for the first time at the Guangzhou Auto Show later this month, but you can let us know what you think of the new NX7 in the comments, today.

#4421. Tesla Cybercab Promises Autonomy for Under $30K, with Some Caveats

The first customers will be required to take delivery in a handful of Texas cities, and the car is currently geofenced to operate only within specific regions.

Earlier this month, Tesla made the surprise announcement that it would wind down production of the polarizing Cybertruck in the middle of next year. A culprit for the Cybertruck’s demise was a much smaller Tesla, the Cybercab, a tiny two-door pod designed to be autonomous and already running as a robotaxi in a few locations. When the Cybercab was revealed in 2024, Tesla promised that the driverless car would be sold to regular customers, and now more details are emerging on that plan.

See all results for used Tesla for sale near 94043

Initially, however, the Cybercab won’t be available to everyone. Late last week, Tesla said that “select customers” would be able to pre-order the Cybercab “for personal use.” Customer deliveries are supposed to kick off by December with a $29,990 starting price.

There are some caveats. That isn’t the final price, as Cybercab owners will also need to pay $299 per month to operate the vehicle, and the Cybercab is currently only able to operate in select geofenced areas, reportedly the same regions where Tesla’s Robotaxi service currently runs. According to tech reviewer Marques Brownlee, who is on the invite list for Cybercab ownership, buyers can also only take delivery in a handful of Texas cities: Austin, Dallas, Fort Worth, Houston, and San Antonio.

This won’t be the case forever, Tesla promises. In response to Brownlee’s post on X, CEO Elon Musk said that the Cybercab “will be available nationwide, as we receive regulatory approval.” He also noted that the current monthly fee is “too high” and said it “should match the cost of Tesla FSD” in the company’s other models, which would put it at around $115 per month. It’s unclear if and when Tesla plans to change the Cybercab’s subscription fee and what changes would have to be made to reduce that cost.

The Cybercab, which was designed without a steering wheel or pedals, is meant to be fully autonomous. It would be the first vehicle sold without driving controls to the general public if Tesla does indeed begin deliveries by the end of 2026. Only a few units should reach customers this year if Tesla does meet its deadlines (a big if), with production ramping up over the course of 2027 once the factory space is freed up by the Cybertruck’s departure.

#4420. China’s electric airliner era starts with a 19-seat plane and 400 km of range

COMAC’s CE-25A, China’s 19-seat battery-electric commuter plane, flew with a crew for the first time on Saturday in Binzhou, Shandong. Two pilots and a flight test engineer were aboard the roughly 10-tonne demonstrator, and COMAC says every system worked normally.

It wasn’t the plane’s first flight. The CE-25A had already completed 19 autonomous test flights with nobody on board since February 2, and China’s aviation regulator is now reviewing it for a type certificate.

The CE-25A is a T-tail commuter plane with 10 electric ducted fans on the wings, five per side, instead of propellers. COMAC lists a 300 km/h cruise speed and a 400 km (250-mile) range.

The CAAC accepting COMAC’s type certificate application starts the airworthiness review. It doesn’t mean paying passengers are close, and COMAC hasn’t given a date for commercial service.

The program has been quiet for a long time. COMAC showed a CE-25A model at the China International Import Expo in Shanghai in November 2023, with a placard listing 400 to 500 km of range and a 400 km/h top cruise speed. The full-size aircraft, registered B-0EFH, only became public when photos leaked on Chinese social media on October 28.

The obvious battery candidate is CATL. In July 2023, COMAC, CATL, and Shanghai Jiao Tong University formed a joint venture with CNY 600 million in registered capital to develop electric aircraft, as we reported when CATL launched its aviation unit.

CATL had just unveiled its “condensed” battery at the time, claiming up to 500 Wh/kg at the cell level, and said it was testing the cells to aviation standards. Neither company has confirmed what’s inside the CE-25A, though.

~500 Wh/kg has long been seen as the target for battery energy density to enable electric flight on a commercial scale.

COMAC isn’t alone in flying a large electric demonstrator. In August, Heart Aerospace flew its X1 in Plattsburgh, New York, for 27 minutes. It’s a 25,000-lb aircraft with a 106-foot wingspan, which Heart calls the largest battery-electric aircraft ever flown.

Eviation flew its 9-passenger Alice back in September 2022, then laid off most of its staff in early 2025.

Heart is the closest Western comparison. It dropped its 19-seat ES-19 for the 30-seat ES-30 back in 2022, and the ES-30 now relies on reserve turbogenerators to stretch its range, with BAE Systems working on the battery. Heart is targeting 2031 for service and claims “more than 40%” lower operating costs.

For years, the go-to excuse in the West for doing nothing about emissions was China. Why should we bother, the argument went, if China won’t? Now China is pulling ahead, and it’s doing it by cutting its dependence on fossil fuels.

Look at trucking. Electric trucks hit 50.3% of China’s heavy truck sales in September, and they’re already eating into the country’s diesel demand. In the US, electric models were about 0.3% of heavy-truck sales last year, according to the ICCT.

A great step in the right direction, probably needs a doubling in range but at current rates of progress that will only be five years away.

Now it’s planes, starting where batteries make sense today: short regional routes. The CE-25A’s 400 km shrinks once you keep the reserves regulators require, and a Beechcraft 1900 turboprop in the same class covers well over 1,000 km. So it’s not replacing turboprops anytime soon. But that’s how trucking started too. Short-haul first, then long-haul tractors once the batteries caught up.

And this couldn’t happen fast enough. We’re in the middle of a diesel and jet fuel crisis. Jet fuel averaged $3.50 a gallon in early August, up 63% from a year earlier, according to Heart Aerospace. Every truck and plane China moves to batteries is one less exposed to that.

China also has the batteries to pull it off, with CATL in the joint venture. Meanwhile, Heart has pushed to 2031 and added a fuel-burning backup, and Eviation is a cautionary tale.

#4419. Robo-frog swims with liquid crystal muscles powered by light

Published Nov 13, 2026 3:00 PM EST

A silicone frog built by engineers at Denmark’s Aarhus University can’t swim nearly as fast as its amphibian inspiration, but it still manages to get the job done without any moving parts. The odd invention owes its slow-but-steady aquatic maneuvering to a set of six artificial muscles specially designed to contract when exposed to near-infrared light.

The team’s novel system is detailed in a study recently published in the journal Advanced Materials Technologies. Although similar setups may one day boost the capabilities of soft robots tasked with search and rescue or environmental monitoring, its creators are a bit more realistic about this frog-bot’s near-term uses.

“I could easily imagine these robots being used as toys before we see them on rescue missions,” Cecilie Ryberg, Aarhus University chemist and study co-author, said in a profile. “I think people would have fun playing with a frog like this using a suitable light source.”

Each of the robot’s muscles is built using crystal elastomers. These materials are specifically manufactured to contract while they are heating, and then revert back to their original shape once cooled. In this case, Ryberg and her collaborators also added a molecule that converts near-infrared light into heat. This allows the muscles to tighten after directly exposing them to a lamp. That said, the process isn’t as simple as sticking the elastomers onto their model frog and dropping it into water.

“Getting the six muscles to work together was a major challenge,” explained Brigitte Städler, a study co-author and Aarhus University chemist. “If they don’t contract in a coordinated way, the frog won’t swim forwards. It may simply spin around.”

A lot of trial-and-error also went into concocting the elastomers themselves. In addition to contracting properly, the material needed the proper consistency to use in a 3D printer. To do this, Ryberg experimented with various molecular ingredients and molecule chain lengths to perfect the robot muscle recipe.

“In a conventional 3D printer, you typically melt a solid plastic filament. Our material is more like very thick syrup or icing that you squeeze through a piping bag when decorating a cake,” said Ryberg.

The final result is a light-powered soft robot that’s quite unique, but also not in any hurry. At its best pace, the frog swam a little over three inches in about two minutes. That may not get it to its destination quickly, but the proof-of-concept successfully offers a new way to think about robotic design, and the ways engineers can power their creations. Until then, there is always the potential for robo-frog toys.

#4418. High altitude, bitter cold, zero drivers: autonomous trucks take on Tibetan mine

Finding qualified equipment operators is hard enough for most mining companies, and the extreme weather, punishing conditions, and oxygen-deprived air of the Tibetan mountains combine to make finding operators even tougher for the operators if this high-altitude copper mine – but SANY thinks they have a solution: fully self-driving haul trucks.

Chinese equipment brand SANY has deployed fully 60 of its 70-tonne (~80 ton) payload-rated SKT105ED battery electric haul trucks at the Zhibula Copper Mine in Tibet. Operated by Zijin Minig and Tibet Julong Copper, the mine functions at a dizzying 17,700 foot elevation in a region of the Gangdese Mountains known as the Kailas Range, and the conditions there would challenge the health and safety of even the toughest and fittest operators.

“High-altitude illness becomes increasingly relevant above 2,500 meters,” explains Eacon, in one section of a published paper. “Research involving workers in Andes mines operating between 3,800 and 4,500 meters found that 73% of workers assessed experienced periods of nocturnal oxygen saturation below 85% during their high-altitude shifts, indicating moderate-to-severe hypoxemia.”

That’s bad news for Zijin’s workers – but the good news here, of course, is that the company won’t be needing many heavy haul drivers going forward.

SANY has been working with Perth, Australia-based Eacon Mining Technology to develop an autonomous haulage solution that uses a full suite of both in-vehicle and ground-based sensors, adaptive vehicle controls, and machine learning that can handle the big bad trucks even here in the Kailas range.

“Autonomous haulage offers one way to address this challenge,” continues the Econ report. “Rather than requiring a driver for each truck, autonomous systems allow fleets to be managed through centralized supervision, with personnel overseeing operations and intervening when required. This reduces the need for people to spend entire shifts operating equipment at elevation, while changing how workforce resources are allocated across the mine … depending on the system configuration, some operations can manage autonomous fleets from remote Integrated Operations Centers located away from the mine site, (allowing) personnel to supervise haulage activities from lower-altitude locations, further reducing the need for workers to remain in extreme-altitude environments.”

The working partnership between the two companies combines SANY’s battery-powered truck platform with Eacon’s full technology stack to create dependable, driverless haul trucks with logic and behaviors that are ideally suited to China’s open-pit mining environments.

Eacon technology is currently operating more than 3,100 autonomous trucks cross more than 40 large-scale mines, including Zijin Mining’s Zijinshan Gold-Copper Mine and at the Norton Gold Fields project in Australia.

While specifications for this specific deployment weren’t disclosed, the SANY SKT105E trucks (the “D” is, presumably, the wide-body variant) the company has deployed elsewhere are powered by a dual-motor electric drivetrain, pairing two permanent-magnet synchronous motors with a dual three-speed automated manual transmission. The system delivers 570 kW (~765 hp) of continuous power and up to 820 kW (~1,100 hp) at peak output, with each motor producing some 2,430 Nm (~18,00 lb-ft) of peak torque.

Those motors get their electrons from an absolute whopper of a lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery pack in capacities ranging from 423 to 642 kWh, depending on configuration. The big trucks also offer regenerative braking to recover energy on downhill runs, while their fast-charging system can reportedly charge the battery from 20% to 90% in under an hour.

#4415. Mowing milestone: Greenzie surpasses 255,000 autonomous miles mowed

Autonomous lawncare specialists Greenzie passed a major milestone with their self-driving mowers last week, surpassing 255,000 cumulative robomowing miles. For context, that’s far enough to mow every inch of space between the Earth and Moon.

Greenzie announced the self-driving milestone last week, and it’s genuinely impressive, reflecting Greenzie Powered Autonomy mowing more than 9 billion (with a b) square feet of turf across more than 200 commercial customers, 45 US states, and more than 500,000 equivalent man-hours of mowing.

And, while I might have pointed the fact that Greenzie mowers have covered more miles in its press release than Daimler’s entire hydrogen truck fleet, the company really seems to be leaning into the Moon angle.

“We mowed to the moon, but the real achievement is the commercial experience behind those miles,” says Charles Brian Quinn, co-founder and CEO of Greenzie and almost definitely the guy who first came up with the lunar lawncare line. “Every mile represents equipment working on real properties with commercial crews. That experience has shaped our technology, strengthened our OEM partnerships and taught us how to help customers successfully integrate autonomy into their daily operations.”

Greenzie develops autonomous packages for, and maintains OEM relationships with electric brands Mean Green Electric Mowers (whose Vanquish Autonomous commercial mower is shown, above), and Greenworks Commercial, as well as gas-powered brands like Bobcat and Wright Manufacturing. Regardless of what powers the mowers, Greenzie supplies the self-driving technology and integration expertise, while its OEM partners develop and manufacture the equipment that does the actual cutting, clearing, and whatever else their clients need.

“Successful autonomy requires more than capable technology,” said Steve Bush, chief operating officer of Greenzie. “Customers need to understand where autonomy fits into their operations, how to prepare their crews and how to measure success. We have spent years learning those lessons alongside our customers and OEM partners, creating a more consistent path to adoption as the industry grows.”

The Mean Green Vanquish Autonomous featured gere is a fully electric, stand-on, zero-turn (ZTR) mower built around an all-day-ready 22 kWh li-ion battery pack and featuring a 60″ rear-discharge mulching deck.

Mean Green claims that the combination of big battery and the electric motors that drive the ZTR mower and spin up its blades are good up to eight hours of continuous mowing on a charge, with an aluminum chassis and deck helping to keep the machine’s overall weight down for easier towing maximum efficiency.

The company says the mower can operate in either manual or autonomous mode, with Greenzie’s self-driving software supported by six depth-sensing stereo cameras providing 360-degree vision, RTK-corrected GPS, and visual-inertial odometry for onboard site mapping and precise positioning, which Greenzie says allows the mower to detect obstacles up to twenty feet away, recognize designated keep-out zones, and automatically return to its starting point when called back.

A top speed of 11.5 mph and the ability to repeat saved mowing routes, the Vanquish is designed to give commercial landscaping crews another productive worker without adding another person to the payroll … which, with a $60,000 asking price, is money they will probably still need.

Let’s get some pro-labor rage going in the comments, and don’t forget to mention what kind of paycheck you’d need to get to go work in landscaping 2,000+ hours a year while you’re there.

#4414. A baby turkey with a feather duster ‘mom’ has a new BFF

Published Nov 14, 2026 10:03 AM EST

It seems straight out of a Disney movie—wild animals from two different species becoming inseparable friends. And yet that’s what happened at the Raven Ridge Wildlife Center in southeastern Pennsylvania, between a turkey and a mourning dove.

Last spring, the wildlife center received two likely orphaned turkey poults (young turkeys). To calm them down, the team put them with a feather-duster as a stand-in mother turkey. Because turkey poults are easily stressed, they are difficult to rehabilitate, according to a Facebook post by the wildlife center. In fact, one of them didn’t make it.

“Since we never raise baby animals alone, we had to find a companion for the remaining poult,” the wildlife center wrote. “We paired it with a baby mourning dove of similar size, hoping they would comfort each other while eating and exploring as they are both ground eaters.”

The pairing turned out to be a raging success. They formed an inseparable bond that Raven Ridge Wildlife Center had never seen before. Months later, the team gave the dove a soft release, meaning the bird could leave whenever it wanted. But he clearly had no intention of leaving his friend. The dove continued returning to the turkey’s cage, and the two would sit near each other on either side of the separation.

“After a few days, we put the dove back in with the turkey, and it was clear they were happiest together,” the wildlife center explained. But “we knew keeping them caged for the rest of their lives, or keeping them just because they were cute, was neither an option nor fair to these wild animals.”

As such, the team contacted a large sanctuary in Pennsylvania to request a joint release. This way, the duo could choose whether to stick together or follow their own paths. After their soft release, the dove flew into the trees and the turkey started foraging, free to stick together or join other members of their species.

“We don’t know if they’ll stay together, but our team made sure they had a safe place until they were ready to be on their own,” the wildlife center concluded.

#4413. Is Tesla rushing out a half-baked Cybercab just to shave MKBHD’s head?

Elon Musk called YouTuber Marques Brownlee “a chicken” early Saturday, hours after Tesla opened invite-only Cybercab orders at $29,990 and Brownlee argued that his famous head-shaving bet isn’t lost.

Tesla has about seven weeks to get a Cybercab into a customer’s hands for under $30,000 before 2027, but the half-baked version of Cybercab that they opened orders for with delivery in December makes it look like it’s just to win this dumb bet.

Surely Tesla isn’t down enough to deliver a half-baked product just to “prove” a YouTuber wrong? Or is it?

After Tesla’s “We, Robot” event in October 2024, Brownlee (MKBHD) said there was no way Tesla would deliver a Cybercab to a customer for $30,000 or less before 2027. If it did, he’d shave his head on camera.

Musk has taken it personally ever since. When the first Cybercab came off the Giga Texas line in February, he replied “Gonna happen 😂” to a bald-MKBHD meme, which we covered at the time. In September, after Brownlee doubled down in a new video, Musk wrote: “I guess he really wants to shave his head 🤷‍♂️”

On Friday, Tesla started inviting “select customers” to buy a Cybercab for personal use. The order page lists $29,990, a mandatory $299 per month Autonomy Subscription, a $1,000 non-refundable deposit, and an estimated delivery of December 2026, only in Tesla’s Texas Robotaxi cities.

As we reported Friday, the car only operates inside Tesla’s Robotaxi geofences. And Tesla’s Cybercab Autonomy Subscription Agreement says it “will not operate” without the $299 plan, bans owners from putting it on the Robotaxi network or using it for ride-hailing, and lets Tesla shrink the operating area at any time.

So Tesla designed a robotaxi, then offered it to select private owners who aren’t allowed to use it as a taxi. Over five years, that’s $47,631 before insurance, registration, and charging. And you are limited to small geofenced areas. If you stop paying Tesla’s monthly fee, which it can change at all times, your cybercab becomes a paperweight.

Brownlee laid out his case Friday night. There are no deliveries yet, the car is invite-only rather than publicly available, and it can’t be used as a cab outside of the existing geofences. He called it “a paperweight if I take this thing home,” though he admits that last point isn’t technically part of the bet.

The memes are everywhere, so let’s go back over the bet: Cybercab publicly available for under $30k by the end of 2026My hair is safe for several reasons1: No deliveries yet. But they’re estimating starting in December so that’s neat2: Invite only, not actually publicly… https://t.co/NCD2aFbe2c

Tesla fans fired back with clips from his September video, where he described a car that “will not ship to regular people like you and me for $30k before the end of 2026.” Whole Mars Catalog, an Elon Musk propagandist whose real name is Omar Qazi, told him to “be a man and honor your word.” Musk reposted it, then replied:

Musk also reposted a Grok answer claiming the current offer “matches” the conditions of the bet.

But around the same time, Musk replied directly to Brownlee’s post about the order page, and it didn’t help Tesla’s case:

“It will be available nationwide, as we receive regulatory approval. But the monthly fee is too high. Should match the cost of Tesla FSD and connectivity for other models, which is more like ~$115/month.”

That’s Tesla’s CEO confirming, a day after launch, that the car can’t be sold outside the areas where it already operates and that its price is wrong. A price that Musk fully controls.

Yes, it looks like Tesla is rushing this out just to win a bet against a Youtuber. Absolutely insane behavior. We’ve seen this movie before. In June 2025, Tesla did a single “autonomous delivery” of a Model Y to meet a Musk deadline, then never did it again.

Tesla always pitched the Cybercab as a vehicle for its Robotaxi network. Now, seven weeks before the deadline, a personal-use version shows up that’s invite-only, Texas-only, banned from doing the one thing it was designed for, and attached to a subscription Musk himself says is too expensive. If you set out to build a product whose main job was letting Musk claim he won a Twitter bet, it would look a lot like this.

This Cybercab offering is completely broken. The value proposition is awful. As others have put it, it’s a permanent variable rate lease starting at $300 a month with a ridiculous $30,000 down payment.

Besides, the bet was "under 30k." Starting price is under 30k, but a subscription is required, which takes it over 30k, just to use it for one day. They could have given the car away for free, and just charged a fee to use it. Doesn't change the total cost.

What do you get for this deal? A 2-seater vehicle that only works in small, incomplete, geo-fenced areas and has no steering wheel to do anything else with it. Meanwhile, Tesla insists that the Model Y, like the ones used in its current Robotaxi service alongside the Cybercab, uses the same self-driving technology.

You can buy one for $40,000, and you get a lot more car than the Cybercab; then you can pay $99 a month for FSD instead of $300 a month. Tesla is supposed to let current Tesla owners drive without supervision in the geo-fenced areas, which would basically be the same product as what Tesla is offering right now with the Cybertruck, but you are not a slave to Tesla, which can brick your car at any time or change the terms.

This offer simply makes no sense, and Musk is sort of admitting it by saying the price should be the same as FSD, not $300 a month.

#4412. The Best Made-in-USA Gifts for Every Person on Your Shopping List

Our car experts choose every product we feature. We may earn money from the links on this page.

From trusted tools to road-trip essentials, we rounded up the toughest gear made in the United States for the car people in your life.

This article was updated in November 2026 with new products and information.

There’s a particular satisfaction in picking up a tool or piece of gear and knowing where it was made. It’s more than patriotism: a pair of boots stitched in Michigan or a kitchen tool forged in Ohio carries a connection to the people and skills behind it.

Buying American-made products helps support the craftspeople, businesses, and communities that keep making things here. And finding those products doesn’t have to be a treasure hunt. We’ve rounded up standout U.S.-made picks for weekend wrenchers, road-trip warriors, and everyone in between.

The Wave is one of Leatherman's most iconic tools, and while it takes on a new shape with the Wave Alpha, it's still the answer when you want one thing that handles 10 small jobs and you don't feel like going back to the toolbox.

This all-in-one tool features one-hand blades, real pliers, actual drivers, a large scissor tool, and more. Leatherman backs it with a no-drama warranty, and their stuff is easy to service if you get it gritty (I've sent in my original Wave for service twice and had it back within a week with little more than the shipping cost to send it out).

Odds are this tool will outlast whoever you give it to, so consider it a long-term investment made right here in the United States.

The brass bolsters and wood handle give the iconic Buck Knives 110 Folding Hunter Knife a significant heft that exudes quality. Made in Post Falls, Idaho, it locks open with a satisfying click and holds an edge through serious cutting tasks. It is not the most high-tech blade on the market, but it is a timeless tool that feels great in the hand.

If you want deep color and gloss for a weekend cruiser, this Griot's Garage Best of Show Wax gets the job done. Formulated just west of Indianapolis, Indiana, it goes on smooth and buffs off without leaving stubborn white dust in the panel gaps.

While it's easy enough to use with a hand buff, it works equally well with an electric buffer if you want to expedite the process. It's affordable, it works well, and overall it delivers a robust shine with a little bit of elbow grease.

The GoRuck GR1 is overkill for a commute, which is exactly why you will like it. Made in America by a veteran-owned company, this bag has straps that are padded perfectly to handle heavy loads, and the laptop compartment is suspended to protect your tech from drops. It opens flat for easy packing and shrugs off rain and abrasions like they are nothing.

I've personally owned one of these for more than 15 years now, and it's been everything from a daily backpack in college to a tool bag that's been used and abused during car repairs. While the 1000D Cordura is certainly faded and the zipper pulls have been replaced a few times, it still performs just as it did on day one.

What's more Americana than a Zippo? Even if you don't smoke, a Zippo is a handy tool to have around (so long as you keep it filled with fluid). The windproof flame works when matches fail, and the tactile click of the lid is oddly satisfying (mine doubles as a fidget toy).

As you'd expect from a brand as synonymous with quality as Channellock, this Tool Roll-5 is the kind of pliers kit that just works, day in and day out. The cutters bite cleanly, the tongue-and-groove jaws actually meet, and the pivots don't wobble after a season of real use.

The included roll keeps everything from clanking around in the trunk or bottoming out in a drawer and is great for keeping forgetful DIYers such as myself from losing them in the middle of projects. As all products on this list, these tools are made in the USA and tough enough to hand to a neighbor without worrying about getting them back bent.

Finding quality local products oftentimes requires giving up a Saturday morning. You have to navigate a farmer's market, walk the stalls, and sift through the inventory to find something worthwhile. The Farmers Finds outsources that legwork by scouring regional markets across the country, buying small-batch goods from independent makers, and packing them into a single box. It’s a straightforward logistical solution akin to a regional community supported agriculture (CSA) box. Instead of driving across state lines to find a specific local preserve or hot sauce, it arrives directly on your porch.You can order a single box, though the subscription model is how the service is really meant to be used. The monthly tier delivers two to four items from a single brand, while the quarterly option scales up to seven to ten products sourced from five different makers. It's a practical gift for someone who appreciates regional goods, but doesn't have the bandwidth to track down the vendors themselves. You get quality American-made products, and the makers get the business.

Smell like you upgraded to a nicer car. Drift infuses a magnetized wood block with clean-ingredient essential oils—teak, amber, and cedar—then snaps it to a low-profile metal visor clip. It's made in the U.S., looks grown-up, and takes quick monthly refill blocks when the scent fades. No dangling trees, no headaches.

If you're looking to pair the Dutch oven with a skillet, or simply don't need the massive capacity of a 5.5-quart pot, the Smithey No. 10 is the logical alternative. Like the rest of their South Carolina-forged lineup, it features a machined, glass-smooth interior that eliminates the stubborn break-in period typical of modern cast iron. It cooks with the non-stick capability of a well-worn vintage piece right out of the box.

The 10-inch diameter hits the sweet spot for daily duty, whether you're searing a pair of ribeyes over an open fire or frying eggs on a kitchen stove, although there are plenty of other sizes available on Smithey's website if you're hoping to go smaller or larger. I'd also recommend picking up a chainmail scrubber to get out the more stubborn food remnants, and Smithey's salt keeper is an adorable accessory to boot.

Having a heavy-duty piece of American metal that takes high heat without warping, wipes clean in seconds, and feels substantial enough to outlast your vehicle fundamentally changes how you operate in the kitchen.

Built just down the road from me in Rockford, Michigan, these Wolverine 1000 Mile Boots are no joke. While they do require a significant break-in period, the payoff is worth the blister or two.

Once the Horween leather molds to your foot, these boots feel like a second skin that look as good as they feel and are tough enough for daily wear. The Goodyear welt construction also means you can resole them in a few years rather than tossing them in the trash when the tread wears down.

What more can I say about Duck Tape Duct Tape that hasn't already been said? Sure, it's never a long-term solution to automotive or home problems, but it'll get the job done until you find a more permanent solution. Hopefully you'll never have to use it, but for 10 bucks or so, it's nice insurance to throw in the trunk for the inevitable emergency.

Duke Cannon's Big Ass Brick of Soap is comically big at first, but then you realize it outlasts three normal ones and doesn't turn into goo in the shower. I've purchased and used a dozen of these over the last decade, and every time I go through a single bar, my spouse has already gone through a three-pack of normal ones.

The scent of this particular bar (they have dozens of scents/formulations to choose from) is more warm "vanilla/wood" than "spill at the distillery," but it does have that signature bourbon smell you'd expect from a little Buffalo Trace.

As a Michigander, I'm a bit biased, but Carhartt Beanies are just a way of life (second only to Stormy Kromers). While not all versions are made in America, there are Woodside Beanies made right here in the States. Just be sure to check the product listing to confirm before making your purchase.

This Rite in the Rain notepad lets you write down torque values, weird part numbers, or your "What's that noise?" notes, all without having to worry about whether the pages will smear if your hands are greasy or it's misting outside.

The covers hold up in a pocket, and the wire doesn't explode into a tangle like some other cheap pads I've used over the years. It's a bit pricey for a small notepad, but when you need a reliable notepad that can take on the elements and solvents, you won't find a better option.

The lifetime warranty is real, but the comfort is why you will keep buying them. Knit in Northfield, Vermont, these Darn Tough Micro Crew Socks breathe well inside a driving shoe or a heavy boot, and the merino wool blend doesn't stink after a long day on the road.

You will have a hard time wearing a hole in a pair, which makes the higher price tag feel like a bargain over the long haul. I've had probably a dozen pair of Darn Tough socks over the years, and I only managed to wear a hole in one, which was only thanks to a little nail sticking out of my home's mid-century wood floors. And, of course, Darn Tough promptly replaced it with a brand-new pair.

This American-made bag takes a beating and looks all the better for it. The rugged twill of the Filson Original Briefcase resists water and wear, while the bridle leather handles soften up nicely over time. It is heavy for what it holds, but it protects a laptop and documents with a style that works as well in a truck as it does in an office.

LED technology revived the classic Maglite form factor you remember from your childhood. Built in Ontario, California, it still has the heft that feels reassuring in your hand, but now it throws a beam that properly lights up the road ahead (or engine beneath you). You get a simple focus twist mechanism, as well as the convenience of D-cell batteries that are easy enough to find at any gas station.

Old leather seats can get stiff and crack over years of use and abuse, but this Leather Honey Leather Conditioner brings them back to life. As its name suggests, this formula—which took home the Best Feel and Finish accolade in our Best Leather Cleaner piece—has a honey-like consistency that makes it easy to wipe on with control. After a few hours of letting it soak in, it leaves behind a clean feel that doesn't leave a greasy residue behind—a major win over cheaper alternatives.

Pouring fluids into a cramped engine bay usually results in a mess, but this FlexAll Flexible Funnel by TEC Products solves that geometry problem.

The nitrile rubber handles oil and gas without degrading, and you can mold it around hoses and wires to create a leak-free path. Sure, it might be a bit more of a hassle to clean when you're done, but the convenience of the gooseneck makes all the difference when trying to get fluids into all the nooks and crannies of modern vehicles.

Most carry-on bags feel flimsy, but the Pelican ATX 22 feels like you could drag it behind the car on the highway and it would survive. Hell, I'm not even sure a particularly grumpy baggage handler could destroy this thing.

The layout is simple, but the injection-molded construction is undeniably Pelican. This particular model is sized just right to fit in the overhead bin without a fight, and you can rest assured clothes and gear will be protected from the elements better than standard fabric luggage ever could manage.

According to the FTC, a product must be “all or virtually all” made in the United States. That means final assembly and significant processing happen in the USA, and nearly all components are made and sourced in the USA.

No. “Assembled in the USA” means the product was put together in the USA, but some parts may come from other countries.

Look for the product’s country-of-origin information and check the manufacturer’s website for details about where it is made, assembled, and sourced.

There are a lot of reasons why, but mainly because shopping U.S.-made goods means you are supporting domestic manufacturers, workers, supply chains.
